messages.subject: Warmup issue with model?
parts:
Hey all,

I've posted about a similar model several times before, but I'm now extending it to normal-theory data.

The model is essentially a CFA model with one latent factor.
The goal is to have a mixture model for each item that allows the item parameters to either be equal across latent groups (if 1 - \Delta_j is high) or to be different across latent groups (if \Delta_j is high).
The likelihood is:


where N is number of cases, J is number of items.
The model aims to find the item parameters, whether an item's parameters are invariant across latent groups or not, and for items that are not invariant, find latent membership probabilities and corresponding item parameters.

I've been working on the dichotomous 2PL version of this for a while now, but I'm extending it to normal-theory models (CFA).

I have priors set for every parameter, and I allow prediction of latent groups (e.g., from demographic data, which sample the person is from, etc). The stan model is at the bottom. Currently I've only implemented K=2 latent groups for the CFA version, so keep that in mind when reading the model; K in the stan code is purely for convenience and readability.

The issue I am having is that chains sometimes set some MAJORLY small step sizes during warmup, and consequently have maximum treedepth on nearly every iteration.
The result is a posterior that's essentially a straight line, because the step sizes are so small. The posterior SD may be about .03.
On simulated datasets, the model will typically work well, with the exception of one chain doing the above.

On 'real' datasets (borrowed from a lab mate), every chain does it, so I get 4 straight lines, all posterior SDs extremely small, massive Rhats, etc.
On the holzinger dataset from lavaan, I sometimes see one chain that does it, and the rest are fine.

I simply cannot figure out why on earth it's doing this, and I welcome any insight.
data {
    int N;
    int J;
    int L;
    int jOrder;
    matrix[N,L] covariates;
    matrix[N,J] y;
   
}

transformed data{
    int K;
    int D;
    K = 2;
    D = 2;
   
}

parameters {
    //Item parameters
    ## change to 0 for non-DIF, since data are scaled?
    vector[J-1] intercept_base[K];
    ordered[K] intercept_ordered;
    vector<lower=0>[J] lambda[K];
    vector<lower=0>[J] residual_s[K];
    vector[J] delta_logit_s;
   
    //Person parameters
    vector[N] theta;
    vector[N] pi_logit_s;
   
    //Softmax parameters
    vector[L] betas_logit;
   
}

transformed parameters {
    vector[J] intercept[K];
    vector[J] delta_logit;
    vector[N] pi_logit;
    vector<lower=0>[J] residual[K];
   
    pi_logit = pi_logit_s + covariates * betas_logit;
   
    delta_logit = delta_logit_s * 3;
   
    //Intercept matrix construction
    for(k in 1:K){
        intercept[k,jOrder] = intercept_ordered[k];
    }
    {
        int skip;
        skip = 0;
       
        for(j in 1:(J-1)){
            if(j == jOrder){skip = skip + 1;}
            intercept[1,j + skip] = intercept_base[1,j];
            intercept[2,j + skip] = intercept_base[2,j];
        }
    }
   
    for(k in 1:K){
        residual[k] = residual_s[k] .* residual_s[k];
    }
   
}

model {
    //Declarations
    vector[K] yhat[J,N];
    vector[2] lp_jnd[J,N];
    vector[2] lp_jndk[J,N];
    vector[N] lp_jn[J];
    vector[J] lp_j;
   
    //Item priors
    for(k in 1:K){
        intercept_base[k] ~ normal(0,1);
        lambda[k] ~ normal(0,1);
        residual_s[k] ~ normal(0,1);
    }
    intercept_ordered ~ normal(0,1);
    delta_logit_s ~ logistic(0,1);
    //Person priors
    theta ~ normal(0,1);
    pi_logit_s ~ logistic(0,1);
    //Softmax priors
    betas_logit ~ logistic(0,1);
   
    //Likelihood
    for(j in 1:J){
        for(n in 1:N){
            for(k in 1:K){
                yhat[j,n,k] = intercept[k,j] + lambda[k,j]*theta[n];
            }
            lp_jnd[j,n,1] = log_inv_logit(-delta_logit[j]) + normal_lpdf(y[n,j] | lambda[1,j]*theta[n], residual_s[1,j]);
            //lp_jnd[j,n,1] = log_inv_logit(-delta_logit[j]) + normal_lpdf(y[n,j] | yhat[j,n,1], residual_s[1,j]);
            lp_jndk[j,n,1] = log_inv_logit(-pi_logit[n]) + normal_lpdf(y[n,j] | yhat[j,n,1], residual_s[1,j]);
            lp_jndk[j,n,2] = log_inv_logit(pi_logit[n]) + normal_lpdf(y[n,j] | yhat[j,n,2], residual_s[2,j]);
            lp_jnd[j,n,2] = log_inv_logit(delta_logit[j]) + log_sum_exp(lp_jndk[j,n]);
            lp_jn[j,n] = log_sum_exp(lp_jnd[j,n]);
        }
        lp_j[j] = sum(lp_jn[j]);
    }
    target += sum(lp_j);
   
}
}

dsComplete <- dsComplete[complete.cases(dsComplete),]
dsComplete <- as.data.frame(scale(dsComplete))

parts:
I didn't go through all the expressions doing the term
calculations, but the overall shape looks right.

Your model has a multiplicative non-identifiability in

lambda[k,j] * theta[n]

because they're both parameters. But this is typical in
a factor model and should be resolved by the priors enough
for the model not to get stuck.

One thing that can happen is that the responsibility goes
all to one cluster, so the delta goes to zero. Can you
see what's happening to the parameter values? Are they running
up against boundaries in the constrained space?

Your delta parameter is getting a flat prior on (0, 1) (delta_logit
gets a logistic(0, 1) in the model). You can make the prior more
peaky and less concentrated around the extremes with a scale << 1.

- Bob

parts:
theta has a normal(0,1) prior on it, and lambda has a half-normal(0,1) prior; I *think* that's identified because the multiplication is different for each individual, and thetas can be negative (same as a CFA with a standardized latent variable and a positivity constraint on loadings).

I don't think the parameters are running up against a constraint. I don't see any issues like that; the 'flat line' posteriors are often near the mean of the non-flat chains, and the non-flat chains don't seem to be bumping up against a value.

I have a logistic(0,1) prior on delta_logit_s, which is then multiplied by 3 (so in essence, delta_logit ~ logistic(0,3)). The reason is actually to encourage classification of items as non-DIF or DIF (high or low Delta values). This is similar to using a beta(.5,.5) prior or so, but it's easier to sample.
Similarly with pi_logit; they are all constructed from pi_logit_s ~ logistic(0,1), but pi_logit = covariates * betas_logit + pi_logit_s; in other words, pi_logit ~ logistic(covariates*betas_logit, 1).
If a certain delta[j] winds up being very high, I would expect that the mixture model component of the likelihood would be what is sampled predominantly. If delta[j] is low, then the extra parameters for the other latent groups would be sampled only from the prior (because they are hardly connected to the likelihood).

When the model has flatlining chains, they have divergences, but only on those flatline chains.

Have you tried setting stepsize lower to begin with? I know it
sounds counterintuitive, but it helps the sampler move around
the Hamiltonian and may get you out of whatever bad place you're
winding up in before adaptation goes off the rails on its own
(the mass matrix gets estimated from draws and step size is
adjusted after that).

- Bob

> I have a logistic(0,1) prior on delta_logit_s, which is then multiplied by 3 (so in essence, delta_logit ~ logistic(0,3)). The reason is actually to encourage classification of items as non-DIF or DIF (high or low Delta values). This is similar to using a beta(.5,.5) prior or so, but it's easier to sample.
> Similarly with pi_logit; they are all constructed from pi_logit_s ~ logistic(0,1), but pi_logit = covariates * betas_logit + pi_logit_s; in other words, pi_logit ~ logistic(covariates*betas_logit, 1).
> If a certain delta[j] winds up being very high, I would expect that the mixture model component of the likelihood would be what is sampled predominantly. If delta[j] is low, then the extra parameters for the other latent groups would be sampled only from the prior (because they are hardly connected to the likelihood).

parts:
I have a sneaking suspicion that it's due to the priors on the residuals. I was wrong, after looking at the trace plots, it seems like flat-lining chains have some residuals flat-lining at 0 with high lambdas. Since that should be impossible, I may need to play with some better lambda and residual priors. Cauchy doesn't work well for residuals *in this model*, because if an item isn't DIF, you have sampling from a prior cauchy and it'll screw up the warmup (I think, since it has infinite variance and no expectation). Because these are standardized data, a cauchy doesn't make sense anyway (can't have residuals greater than 1; the total variance of each variable can't exceed 1). half-normal seems to allow 0 residuals, which may cause the flatlining. I'm going to play with gamma-distributed lambdas and gamma-distributed residuals and report back.

Any other thoughts are of course welcome.

The latest: I changed the ordering constraint from some item's intercepts ordered across groups to slopes across groups, and that helped with one dataset (sped up the model considerably too, probably because there's more separation in slopes than in intercepts for standardized variables).

One dataset is still not working with the model (flatlining). I'm wondering if it's due to the distribution of the variables though.
Some variables are SEVERELY positively skewed, and moreover, it's likert-type output. So some items have a histogram of, e.g., 90 5 6 10 6 7.
I'm guessing that when fitting that data to a mixture, it's creating two classes: one which only responds '1' and another which responds 2,3,4,5,6. However, the problem is that for those in the '1' latent group have predicted scores with 0 potential variance, and the resulting likelihood is probably N(1,.000001), causing a massive spike in the posterior and causing the chains to fail.

I think the way out of it is to use a graded response model for this type of data instead of a normal-theory CFA (not that you *should* use CFA for such severely skewed data anyway).

I'll take a stab at my first GRM for stan tomorrow. My eyes are bleeding from working on this all day.
